title: Agents That Pay: Issuers Must Know Your Agent
subtitle: Card networks are live with AI agents in the UAE. Issuing banks need a control model for delegated spending.
intro: AI agents that buy things on a customer's behalf have moved from demonstration to live transactions in the UAE, led by the card networks. The commercial debate focuses on merchants and networks, but the hardest questions land on issuing banks: who authorised this payment, within what limits, and who pays when the agent gets it wrong. Our argument is that issuers need a know-your-agent discipline, covering delegated authority, tokenised credentials, liability and oversight, before agent-initiated volume becomes material, rather than improvising it through disputes afterwards.

sections.heading: The UAE is an early proving ground
sections.body: Two prominent early agentic-payment deployments involve UAE counterparts. Visa announced on 18 December 2025 that it was working with Aldar so that customers in the UAE could use AI agents to pay recurring real-estate service charges. Visa said that hundreds of agent-initiated transactions had been completed with more than 100 partners, and said it expected millions of consumers to be using AI agents to make purchases by the 2026 holiday season. Mastercard, for its part, launched Agent Pay in the UAE with Majid Al Futtaim, starting with VOX Cinemas. The use cases are telling. Recurring service charges and cinema tickets are bounded, repeatable purchases with a known merchant and a predictable amount, precisely where delegation is lowest risk. They are the equivalent of standing orders with more intelligence. The next wave will be less bounded: agents that compare suppliers, choose between merchants, negotiate timing and split payments across instruments. For issuers, the lesson from the first deployments is that the infrastructure is arriving through the networks whether or not the bank has a view, and that customers will judge the bank on how it behaves when an agent's purchase is disputed.

sections.heading: Four questions every issuer must answer
sections.body: Know-your-agent is the natural extension of know-your-customer to a world in which the entity initiating a payment is software acting for a customer. It raises four questions. First, delegated authority: what exactly did the customer authorise the agent to do, for which merchants or categories, up to what amount and for how long, and how is that mandate recorded in a form that can be evidenced later? Second, credentials: an agent should never hold a customer's primary card details; it should transact with a tokenised credential scoped to the agent and the mandate, which the issuer can suspend without reissuing the customer's card. Third, liability: when an agent buys the wrong item, overspends, or is manipulated by a malicious website, the dispute will arrive at the issuer, and the allocation of loss between customer, agent provider, merchant and bank is not yet settled in most rulebooks. Fourth, authentication: step-up challenges designed for a human at a checkout do not work when the human is absent, so the issuer needs rules for when an agent transaction must return to the customer for confirmation. None of these questions is exotic. Each has an analogue in existing card, mandate and dispute processes, which is where issuers should start.

sections.heading: Oversight models already exist in UAE guidance
sections.body: Banks do not need to invent a governance vocabulary for agents. The CBUAE's February 2026 guidance on responsible AI sets out three oversight models: human in the loop, human on the loop, and human out of the loop, with the last reserved for low-risk processes. It also gives customers rights to an explanation, to challenge and to redress, and confirms that licensed institutions remain accountable for AI they outsource. These map cleanly onto agentic payments. A customer confirming each purchase an agent proposes is human in the loop. An agent paying recurring bills within a standing mandate, with the customer notified and able to intervene, is human on the loop. Fully autonomous spending without notification should, on the CBUAE's logic, be confined to low-risk, low-value cases. The accountability point matters most. Where a bank offers its own agent, or allows third-party agents to transact on its credentials, it cannot disclaim responsibility for how the agent behaves by pointing to the provider. An issuer's agent policy should therefore state, for each class of agent transaction, which oversight model applies, how the customer is informed in Arabic and English, and how a disputed agent payment is explained and remedied.

sections.heading: Temper the upside with realism
sections.body: The prize is large enough to justify investment. BCG estimated in March 2026 that AI agents could raise retail-bank profitability by 30% and reduce costs by 30 to 40% by 2030. In our view much of that value will sit inside the bank, in servicing, operations and credit, rather than in customer-facing shopping agents, but payments are where customers will first experience agents acting on their money. The failure rate is also likely to be high. Gartner predicted in June 2025 that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027. Our reading is that both statements can be true. Agentic programmes that start from a technology demonstration and search for a use case will be cancelled; those that start from a bounded, measurable process, with controls designed in, will compound. For issuers, that argues for a sequence: begin with low-risk, mandate-based agent payments such as recurring bills and subscriptions, instrument them thoroughly, learn how disputes and customer complaints behave, and only then extend delegated authority to open-ended purchasing.

sections.heading: An issuer's agenda for 2027
sections.body: We would prioritise five actions. First, define an agent mandate standard: the minimum data an issuer requires to record what a customer delegated, including scope, limits, duration and revocation, and make it visible and editable in the banking app. Second, require tokenised, agent-specific credentials for all agent transactions and build the ability to suspend an agent without disrupting the customer's other payments. Third, extend fraud and dispute processes to treat the agent as a distinct actor, with reason codes for agent error, agent manipulation and mandate breach, and agree liability positions with network and merchant partners before volumes grow. Fourth, adopt the CBUAE's three oversight models as the policy language for agent payments, with a clear rule for which transactions require customer confirmation, and bilingual notifications for every agent-initiated payment. Fifth, run a contained pilot in a bounded use case, with explicit success and stop criteria, so the programme does not join the projects Gartner expects to be cancelled. Under the 5E lens this is Experience and Execution: letting customers delegate with confidence because the bank can prove what was authorised and put things right when an agent fails.

keyTakeaways: Visa with Aldar and Mastercard Agent Pay with Majid Al Futtaim put UAE issuers among the first to face agent-initiated payments.
Know-your-agent covers four issues: delegated authority, tokenised credentials, liability allocation and authentication without the customer present.
The CBUAE's in-the-loop, on-the-loop and out-of-the-loop models give issuers a ready vocabulary for agent oversight.
Start with bounded, mandate-based payments and explicit stop criteria; Gartner expects over 40% of agentic projects to be cancelled.

title: Aani Is Not a Cost Centre
subtitle: Instant payments as a revenue line and a data asset for UAE banks, if they build for it
intro: Most UAE banks connected to Aani because they had to. The rail is now large enough that treating it as mandated plumbing is a strategic error. With 12.5 million users and roadmap features that reach into direct debits, business payments and cross-border remittance, Aani and the parallel Open Finance framework are becoming the channel through which account-to-account commerce in the UAE will run. Our argument: the banks that win will treat instant payments as a product and a real-time data feed, and will build the fraud, data and API capabilities to monetise both.

sections.heading: The scale case is already made
sections.body: The adoption numbers, published by Al Etihad Payments on 10 April 2026, settle the question of whether Aani matters. The platform had reached 12.5 million users and around 774,000 merchants. Roughly 25,000 transfers a day were being made using only a mobile number, the average transfer completed in three seconds, transfer volumes had grown six-fold year on year, and growth had averaged 10% a month through 2025. Seventy-four licensed financial institutions were connected, including 85% of banks, but only 10% of exchange houses and 5% of wallets and finance companies. Two points follow for bank strategy. First, the rail is mainstream: a bank whose customers cannot pay and be paid instantly by mobile number is visibly behind. Second, the long tail of non-bank participants is still to connect, which means the competitive field around Aani will widen rather than narrow. AEP's stated roadmap at the time included cross-border payments, electronic direct debit, e-cheques and business-to-business payments. Each of those moves Aani from person-to-person convenience into territory where banks currently earn fees and hold relationships, from salary and supplier payments to recurring collections.

sections.heading: Where the revenue is
sections.body: Instant payments compress transaction fees; they do not eliminate value. The value moves to the services wrapped around the payment. For merchants and corporates, electronic direct debit and business-to-business capability create a case for bank-branded collection products: request-to-pay journeys, automated reconciliation, and real-time cash visibility sold as treasury services rather than priced per transfer. For retail customers, the payment moment is the natural point for embedded credit, savings sweeps and loyalty. Cross-border is the clearest near-term prize. AEP selected Montran in March 2026 to build an International Remittance Platform gateway linking Aani first to India's UPI, with real-time ISO 20022 message transformation, and the UAE is home to around 3.5 million Indian nationals. A bank that designs a remittance proposition around that corridor, with transparent pricing and instant delivery, competes directly with exchange houses on their core business. Open Finance widens the opportunity further. FAB and Pay10 went live with retail Pay by Bank in December 2025 under Nebras governance, Commercial Bank of Dubai was described in January 2026 as the first UAE bank to fully activate Open Finance in live operations, and ADIB became the first Islamic bank to implement it under AlTareq the same month.

sections.heading: The data asset most banks are not using
sections.body: Every instant payment carries structured information about who paid whom, when, and increasingly why. Where messages follow the ISO 20022 standard, that information is richer and more consistent than in legacy formats, and Open Finance consent flows add permissioned access to data held at other institutions. Taken together, this is the most current view of customer cash flow a bank has ever had. It can power better underwriting for small businesses whose invoices and receipts move over the rail, earlier identification of financial stress in retail customers, merchant analytics products, and more precise pricing. Most banks, however, still land payments data in overnight batches, into warehouses designed for reporting rather than decisions. The result is that a three-second payment informs a credit or marketing decision the following day, if at all. Capturing the value requires a real-time data layer that streams payment events, enriches them with counterparty and category information, and serves them to decision engines and product teams through governed interfaces. Platforms such as Microsoft Fabric can provide this streaming and analytics layer, but the harder work is organisational: agreeing data ownership, consent handling and quality standards so that payments data can be trusted in credit and customer decisions.

sections.heading: Fraud must be co-deployed, not bolted on
sections.body: The same speed that makes Aani attractive makes it attractive to fraudsters. ACI Worldwide's Scamscope research, published in December 2024, estimated UAE authorised push payment scam losses at US$8.3 million in 2023 and projected US$30.3 million by 2028, and found that one in five scam victims leave their bank. Industry evidence on AI-enabled fraud points the same way: in the ACFE and SAS 2026 benchmarking study, 77% of respondents reported increased deepfake social engineering. Every new Aani capability widens the surface. Mobile-number transfers make it easier to send money to a stranger; direct debits create mandate fraud risk; business payments invite invoice redirection; cross-border links extend the reach of mule networks. The implication is that fraud controls should be designed into each new product at the same time, not retrofitted after losses appear. The real-time data layer described above is also the fraud layer: the same payment events, enriched with device, behaviour and network signals, feed both the product and the risk decision. Banks that build these separately will pay twice and still have gaps between them.

sections.heading: What banks should build in 2027
sections.body: We would frame the agenda around five commitments. First, appoint a product owner for instant payments with a revenue target, not only an uptime target, and a roadmap aligned to AEP's direct-debit, business-payment and cross-border plans. Second, build a real-time payment event stream, enriched and governed, that product, credit and fraud teams consume from a single source, and retire overnight batch dependencies for decision use cases. Third, prepare a cross-border proposition for the UAE–India corridor that can launch as soon as the UPI link is available to participants, with pricing and delivery promises that compete with exchange houses. Fourth, treat Open Finance as a distribution channel: publish reliable, well-documented APIs, partner deliberately with third-party providers on Pay by Bank, and use consented data to improve underwriting. Fifth, co-deploy fraud controls with every new capability, including payee name checks, mandate monitoring for direct debits and mule-account detection, and measure scam losses per million transactions alongside revenue. Federal Decree-Law 6 of 2025 has made open finance and digital-wallet activities licensable, so the competitive set will grow. In 5E terms, this is Empowerment and Evolution: turning a regulatory connection into a platform that keeps generating products.

keyTakeaways: Aani had 12.5 million users and 774,000 merchants by April 2026; it is now core infrastructure, not a pilot.
Value moves from transfer fees to collections, treasury, embedded credit and cross-border services wrapped around the payment.
Real-time payment events are the freshest cash-flow data a bank has; most still process them overnight.
Build fraud controls into every new Aani capability from day one; the same data layer should serve product and risk.

title: Deepfakes at the Front Door
subtitle: Synthetic identities and instant rails leave GCC banks seconds to decide. Most controls were built for days.
intro: Two trends are converging on GCC banks. Generative AI has made it cheap to fake a face, a voice or a document convincingly enough to pass remote onboarding and social-engineer a payment. At the same time, instant rails such as the UAE's Aani settle transfers in about three seconds, removing the recovery window that fraud operations have always relied on. Our argument is that the answer is not more friction everywhere, but better signals at two moments that matter, onboarding and payment authorisation, and deliberate friction only where risk concentrates.

sections.heading: The attack has moved to the front door
sections.body: The evidence from fraud practitioners is stark. The ACFE and SAS 2026 Anti-Fraud Technology Benchmarking Report, published on 25 March 2026 and based on 713 respondents, found that 77% had seen an increase in deepfake-enabled social engineering and 72% an increase in deepfake digital injection attacks, in which synthetic images or video are fed directly into a verification flow rather than presented to a camera. Only 7% described their organisations as more than moderately prepared for AI-fuelled fraud. These two attack types map onto the two front doors of a retail bank. Digital injection targets onboarding: a synthetic or stolen identity is used to open an account that later receives and moves proceeds. Deepfake social engineering targets authorisation: a genuine customer is persuaded, by a convincing voice or video of someone they trust, to approve a payment themselves. Neither is stopped by strong authentication, because in the first case the credential is issued to the fraudster and in the second the legitimate customer authenticates correctly. Controls that ask only whether the right person logged in will pass both.

sections.heading: Instant rails change the economics of recovery
sections.body: The UAE is scaling real-time payments quickly. Al Etihad Payments reported in April 2026 that Aani had reached 12.5 million users, around 774,000 merchants and 74 connected licensed financial institutions, with transfers averaging three seconds and volumes up six-fold year on year. This is a genuine public good, and it also changes the fraud equation. In a three-second payment there is no batch window in which an analyst can review an alert, and no practical opportunity to recall funds once a mule account has forwarded them. Authorised push payment scams are the natural beneficiary. ACI Worldwide's Scamscope research, published in December 2024, estimated UAE APP scam losses at US$8.3 million in 2023 and projected US$30.3 million by 2028. The same research found that one in five scam victims leave their bank. That last figure deserves attention in the boardroom: the cost of scams is not only the reimbursed or written-off loss, but the customer relationship. A bank that is seen to have waved a payment through to a fraudster rarely keeps the customer, whatever the legal position on liability.

sections.heading: The explainability gap will become a supervisory issue
sections.body: Banks are turning to AI to fight AI, but slowly and with an unresolved weakness. In the ACFE and SAS study, 25% of organisations used AI or machine learning in anti-fraud, up from 18% in 2024. Some 82% said explainability was a priority, yet only 6% were confident they could explain their AI's decisions. In the UAE, that gap has regulatory consequences. The CBUAE's February 2026 guidance on responsible AI gives customers rights to an explanation, to challenge and to redress, and expects Arabic and English disclosures. A model that blocks a salary transfer or declines to onboard a customer without a reason the bank can articulate is a complaint, and potentially a finding, waiting to happen. Supervisory expectations around financial crime are also tightening. On 24 June 2026 the CBUAE fined a foreign bank branch AED 20 million for significant and repeated AML, CFT and sanctions failures and fined its Head of Compliance and MLRO AED 300,000 personally. Internationally, the FATF's new President, Giles Thomson, has named the international response to fraud, including the laundering of proceeds from scam compounds, as his first priority for his July 2026 to June 2028 term.

sections.heading: Better signals, targeted friction
sections.body: The design principle we recommend is to separate detection from friction. Detection should be continuous and largely invisible. At onboarding, that means liveness and injection-attack detection that inspects the capture pipeline itself, device and session intelligence, and consistency checks between the claimed identity and its digital footprint. At authorisation, it means behavioural signals, such as hesitation, unusual navigation or an active phone call during a banking session, alongside payee risk. The most valuable signal is often in the network rather than the transaction: a new beneficiary account that has received small credits from many unrelated senders, or that shares devices and contact details with known mule accounts, is visible only when a bank resolves entities across its own data and connects them. Entity-resolution platforms such as Quantexa exist for exactly this purpose. Friction should then be applied sparingly and deliberately: a confirmation-of-payee style name check on first payments to new beneficiaries, a short hold or call-back on high-risk first-time transfers, and in-app warnings written for the specific scam typology the signals suggest. Speed should remain the default; delay should be earned by evidence.

sections.heading: Actions for the next two quarters
sections.body: We would ask bank executives to commission five pieces of work. First, map fraud controls against the two front doors separately, onboarding and authorisation, and test each against deepfake injection and deepfake social engineering scenarios rather than generic fraud. Second, bring mule-account detection into the same view as payment fraud, because in instant payments the receiving account is the last point of control. Third, define a risk-based friction policy for Aani and other instant payments: which combinations of new payee, amount, behavioural anomaly and network risk trigger a name check, a warning, a hold or a call-back, with target decision times in milliseconds. Fourth, set an explainability standard for every fraud and onboarding model, so that each decline or hold produces a reason code a customer-service agent can explain in Arabic or English and a customer can challenge. Fifth, measure what matters: scam losses and reimbursements, false-positive friction per thousand payments, and attrition among scam victims. Under the 5E lens this is Experience and Efficiency together, keeping instant payments instant for the vast majority while concentrating effort where the evidence says fraud is.

keyTakeaways: Deepfakes attack two doors: injection at onboarding and social engineering at authorisation. Strong authentication stops neither.
Three-second settlement removes the recovery window; detection must happen before the payment, not after.
Only 6% of anti-fraud practitioners are confident explaining AI decisions, a gap CBUAE customer-explanation rights will expose.
Keep detection continuous and invisible; apply name checks, holds and call-backs only where network and behavioural risk concentrate.

title: The GCC's AI Constraint Is People, Not Models
subtitle: The first Evident index for the Middle East and Africa shows ambition at the top and a thin talent bench
intro: GCC banks now appear on an international AI leaderboard, and the region's leaders score close to one another. The more important finding sits beneath the rankings: the pool of people who build AI in the region's banks is about half the size of global benchmarks. Models are increasingly available to everyone through cloud platforms and partners. What differentiates banks is the capacity to turn models into governed, adopted products. Our argument is that the binding constraint on GCC bank AI is operating model and talent, and that closing it requires deliberate design rather than more pilots.

sections.heading: What the index says
sections.body: Evident published its inaugural AI Index for Banks covering the Middle East and Africa on 2 June 2026. Emirates NBD ranked first of the 25 banks assessed, followed by Standard Bank, First Abu Dhabi Bank and Nedbank, with the leading four all within one point of each other on a 100-point scale. The index scores banks on four pillars: Talent, Innovation, Leadership and Transparency, and FAB led the Transparency pillar. Evident's key-findings report adds three points that matter more than the ranking itself. The region's AI-development talent pool is about half the size of global bank benchmarks. The 25 banks documented more than 50 AI use cases over two years. And 14 of the 25 had contributed to their national AI strategies, reflecting how closely bank AI in the region is tied to government agendas. Read together, the findings describe a sector with strong executive intent and visible activity, but thin delivery capacity. When the top of a leaderboard is that tightly bunched, the next few years will be decided less by announcements than by which banks can build, deploy and run AI at scale with the people they have.

sections.heading: Leadership signals are strengthening
sections.body: Banks are responding at the top. On 21 August 2026 ADIB appointed Pedro Uria-Recio, formerly of CIMB, as Chief AI Officer to deploy generative and agentic AI across the bank. ADIB serves 2.7 million customers and reports that 94% of its transactions are digital, which gives an AI leader a large base of digital journeys and data to work with. Emirates NBD, meanwhile, was reported in July 2026 to be partnering with Techstars to back start-ups working on agentic finance, a way of importing ideas and specialist talent that the bank does not need to employ directly. These moves are welcome, and they also illustrate the limit of leadership on its own. A Chief AI Officer can set direction, prioritise use cases and hold the bank to account, but cannot personally close a talent gap measured across the sector. Accountability below the top is also uneven. The DFSA's AI survey of November 2025 found that 52% of DIFC firms were using AI, but 21% lacked clear accountability for it. Appointing a senior AI executive is a necessary signal; building the teams, ownership and routines beneath that executive is the work that determines results.

sections.heading: Why operating model beats model choice
sections.body: The instinct in many banks is to frame AI as a technology selection: which foundation model, which cloud, which vendor. Those decisions matter, but they are converging. Leading models are available through the major cloud providers, and regional capacity is expanding. What does not converge is the organisation around the model. A bank needs product owners who can define a problem worth solving, data engineers who can deliver trustworthy inputs, model risk specialists who can validate and monitor, and business teams willing to change a process. Where any of those is missing, pilots stall. Gartner predicted in June 2025 that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027. The forecast points to a familiar diagnosis: AI programmes rarely fail because the model was wrong. They fail because the operating model around it could not carry the work into production.

sections.heading: Building capability with a thin bench
sections.body: A talent pool half the size of global benchmarks rules out simply hiring a large central team of specialists. GCC banks need a design that makes scarce experts go further. We see four elements. First, a small central AI centre of excellence that owns platforms, standards, model risk and reusable components, so that each new use case does not start from nothing. Second, cross-functional product teams embedded in business lines, each owning a portfolio of AI use cases end to end, with the centre providing specialists on rotation. Third, systematic upskilling: the largest pool of potential AI capacity in any bank is its existing analysts, engineers, risk and operations staff, and structured academies can convert a meaningful share of them into practitioners and informed users. Automation platforms such as UiPath can help here, letting operations teams build and run agentic workflows within guardrails the centre defines. Fourth, deliberate use of partners to supply scarce skills for defined periods, with knowledge transfer written into every engagement so that capability stays in the bank. The aim is a bank that depends less on individual experts and more on repeatable ways of working.

sections.heading: Five actions for bank leadership
sections.body: We would ask boards and executive committees to commission the following. First, a talent baseline: how many people in the bank can build, validate, deploy and operate AI today, compared with the use-case pipeline the strategy assumes. Most banks have not measured this, and the Evident findings suggest the answer will be sobering. Second, a named accountable executive for every AI use case in production or pilot, closing the kind of accountability gap the DFSA survey identified. Third, an operating-model decision on the centre of excellence and embedded product teams, with clear decision rights over platforms, data and model risk. Fourth, an upskilling programme with targets for converting existing staff into AI practitioners, in Arabic and English, tied to real use cases rather than generic training. Fifth, a portfolio discipline for AI investment, with explicit stop criteria for pilots that do not reach production, so that scarce talent is concentrated on what is working. Through the 5E lens this is Empowerment and Evolution: equipping people to use AI well and building an organisation that improves its AI capability every year rather than depending on a handful of hires.

keyTakeaways: Emirates NBD topped Evident's first MEA bank AI index, with the leading banks within one point of each other.
The region's bank AI-development talent pool is about half the size of global benchmarks; that is the binding constraint.
AI programmes rarely fail on model choice; they fail on ownership, data culture and the path to production.
Combine a lean centre of excellence, embedded product teams, large-scale upskilling and partners who transfer knowledge.

title: The EU AI Act Was Not Delayed. Part of It Was.
subtitle: Why GCC banks should spend the high-risk reprieve building one AI control framework, not waiting
intro: The EU's Digital Omnibus has been widely read as a pause on the AI Act. It is not. The deadline for stand-alone high-risk systems, including credit scoring, has moved to 2 December 2027, but the Act's transparency obligations were left untouched. For GCC banks with European customers, branches or counterparties, the reprieve is real but narrow. Our argument is simple: the extra time is best spent building a single AI control framework that satisfies Brussels, the CBUAE and SDAIA at once, rather than three parallel compliance programmes that will each be rebuilt when the next rule lands.

sections.heading: What actually changed, and what did not
sections.body: The omnibus reached provisional political agreement on 7 May 2026 and received the Council's final approval on 29 June 2026; it was reported to have been published in the Official Journal on 24 July and to have entered into force on 27 July. Its headline effect is a new timetable for high-risk AI. Stand-alone systems listed in Annex III, the category that covers creditworthiness assessment and credit scoring, now face obligations from 2 December 2027. AI embedded in regulated products moves to 2 August 2028. The deadline for national regulatory sandboxes moved to 2 August 2027, and the AI-literacy duty under Article 4 was softened. What did not move matters as much. According to Gibson Dunn's analysis, the Article 50 transparency obligations are unaffected and proceed as originally scheduled. Those are, broadly, the duties that touch customers most directly, such as telling people they are interacting with an AI system, and labelling synthetic content. A GCC bank running a generative-AI assistant for EU-resident clients, or producing AI-generated marketing aimed at them, has no additional runway on that front. The myth of a general delay is therefore not just inaccurate; it is operationally dangerous, because it invites programme sponsors to de-prioritise precisely the obligations that remain live.

sections.heading: The GCC has already written its own rulebook
sections.body: Waiting for Europe also ignores what regional supervisors have already done. The CBUAE's Guidance Note on consumer protection and the responsible adoption of AI and machine learning, issued in February 2026, is principles-based but specific in its expectations. It rests on five principles: governance and accountability, fairness, transparency and explainability, human oversight, and data management and privacy. It sets out three oversight models, human in the loop, human on the loop and human out of the loop, and confines the last to low-risk processes. It requires disclosures in Arabic and English, gives customers rights to an explanation, to challenge and to redress, and makes clear that licensed financial institutions remain accountable for AI they outsource. In Saudi Arabia, SDAIA's National AI Risk Management Framework, published in 2026, prescribes a staged risk cycle, a four-by-four likelihood and impact matrix and seven risk categories, while SDAIA has assigned SAMA to ensure that its licensed entities comply with the Personal Data Protection Law. Internationally, the Financial Stability Board consulted in June 2026 on twelve sound practices for the responsible adoption of AI by financial institutions, with comments closing on 22 July. The direction of travel across all of these is the same: inventory, risk-tier, explain, oversee, evidence.

sections.heading: One framework, many regulators
sections.body: The practical implication is that a GCC bank does not need an EU AI Act programme, a CBUAE programme and a SAMA programme. It needs one control framework with regulator-specific mappings. The core artefacts overlap almost entirely. A model and use-case inventory serves the EU's high-risk classification, the CBUAE's oversight-model choice and SDAIA's risk categories. A risk-tiering method, calibrated to SDAIA's likelihood and impact matrix, can drive which systems require human-in-the-loop controls under CBUAE guidance and which would qualify as Annex III high-risk in Europe. Explainability standards written once for credit decisions will serve a UAE customer's right to an explanation and an EU applicant's expectations alike. Third-party AI clauses that preserve accountability for outsourced models satisfy the CBUAE and anticipate what European supervisors will ask. The alternative is expensive. Banks that build to each rulebook separately end up with duplicated inventories that disagree, inconsistent risk ratings for the same model and control testing that cannot be reused. When the FSB's sound-practices work and future Gulf rules add requirements, a unified framework absorbs them as mapping changes; a fragmented one requires another project.

sections.heading: The accountability gap is the real exposure
sections.body: The weakest link is rarely the model. It is the question of who owns it. The DFSA's AI survey, published on 12 November 2025 with 661 respondents, found that 52% of DIFC firms were using AI, up from 33% a year earlier, and that 21% lacked clear accountability for AI. Adoption is running ahead of governance. That gap matters more under the new UAE framework than it did before: Federal Decree-Law 6 of 2025 makes responsible managers personally liable, and the CBUAE has shown in 2026 that it will pursue individuals as well as institutions for control failures. A bank whose AI inventory lists models without named business owners, validated risk tiers and documented oversight models is carrying exposure that no amount of model accuracy will offset. Our view is that the extra year the omnibus has given to Annex III systems should be used primarily to close this ownership gap, because it is the precondition for everything the European, Emirati and Saudi frameworks ask for, and because it is the part of AI governance that takes longest to embed in a large organisation.

sections.heading: What to do before 2 December 2027
sections.body: We would prioritise five actions. First, treat Article 50 transparency as current: audit every customer-facing generative-AI touchpoint and synthetic-content workflow that reaches EU residents, and confirm disclosure is in place now. Second, build a single AI inventory with a named accountable executive for every use case, tagged with its CBUAE oversight model, its SDAIA risk rating and its EU classification where relevant. Third, identify which credit, pricing and eligibility models would fall within Annex III and run them through a gap assessment against high-risk requirements in 2026 and early 2027, leaving time to remediate data lineage, documentation and human oversight before the deadline. Fourth, write one explainability standard for adverse credit decisions, bilingual by design, that can generate the customer explanation the CBUAE expects and the documentation a European supervisor would request. Fifth, amend vendor contracts so that outsourced AI comes with audit rights, model documentation and incident notification. In 5E terms this is Execution and Evolution: governance that ships with the model and adapts as rules change, rather than a compliance exercise restarted every time a regulator publishes.

keyTakeaways: The omnibus moved Annex III high-risk deadlines, including credit scoring, to 2 December 2027; Article 50 transparency duties did not move.
CBUAE guidance, SDAIA's framework and the FSB's sound-practices work share one logic: inventory, tier, explain, oversee, evidence.
Build one AI control framework with regulator-specific mappings rather than parallel compliance programmes.
Use the reprieve to close the accountability gap: every AI use case needs a named owner and a documented oversight model.

title: When the MLRO Is Fined: Rules Alone Won't Protect You
subtitle: Personal liability and a fraud-first FATF agenda call for network-led detection and explainable case evidence
intro: On 24 June 2026 the CBUAE fined a foreign bank branch AED 20 million for significant and repeated AML, CFT and sanctions failures, and fined its Head of Compliance and MLRO AED 300,000 personally. Days earlier, FATF had added Iraq to its grey list, and its incoming president has since made fraud his first priority. Together these developments change the question an MLRO must answer. It is no longer enough to show that monitoring rules exist and alerts were worked. The MLRO must be able to show that the bank understood who it was dealing with and why each decision was reasonable.

sections.heading: The personal cost of control failure
sections.body: The June 2026 penalty is notable less for the institutional fine than for the individual one. By sanctioning the MLRO directly, the Central Bank signalled that it regards the effectiveness of the financial crime framework as a personal responsibility, not only a corporate one. This follows earlier enforcement of real scale, including an AED 200 million penalty on an exchange house in May 2025, and it sits alongside Article 181 of the new Central Bank law, under which responsible managers can be held personally liable. For an MLRO, the implication is uncomfortable. A monitoring programme can be fully documented, well staffed and compliant on paper, and still fail to detect activity that a supervisor later judges obvious in hindsight. When that happens, the defence that rules were in place and alerts were closed within service levels is unlikely to be persuasive. What protects the MLRO is evidence that the bank's detection approach was capable of seeing the risk and that decisions were taken on a complete picture.

sections.heading: The threat has moved to networks and to fraud
sections.body: FATF's June 2026 plenary, held from 17 to 19 June, added Iraq and Bosnia and Herzegovina to the list of jurisdictions under increased monitoring, removed Algeria and Namibia, and consulted on guidance for Recommendation 16 on payment transparency. Giles Thomson of the United Kingdom, who took over as FATF President in July 2026 for a term running to June 2028, has named the international response to fraud, including the laundering of proceeds from scam compounds, as his first priority. For UAE banks, Iraq's listing raises the due diligence burden on a set of relationships and trade flows that matter to the region. The fraud priority matters just as much. ACI Worldwide's Scamscope analysis estimated UAE authorised push payment scam losses at US$8.3 million in 2023 and projected US$30.3 million by 2028. Scam proceeds are rarely moved by one account acting alone; they pass through networks of mules, shell entities and linked counterparties designed to stay beneath single-account thresholds.

sections.heading: Why rules-based monitoring leaves the MLRO exposed
sections.body: Traditional transaction monitoring evaluates accounts and transactions largely in isolation against thresholds and scenarios. It is good at catching known patterns in single accounts and poor at seeing relationships. A mule network in which each account moves modest sums, or a trade-based scheme spread across several corporate customers sharing directors, addresses or devices, can pass through a rules engine without generating a meaningful alert. Meanwhile, the same engine generates large volumes of false positives, consuming analyst time on activity that is plainly benign. The industry's preparedness is limited. In the ACFE and SAS 2026 Anti-Fraud Technology Benchmarking Report, only 7 per cent of 713 respondents described themselves as more than moderately prepared for AI-fuelled fraud, while 77 per cent reported increased deepfake social engineering. The weakness is not effort but perspective. A system that cannot resolve that three customer records are the same person, or that several apparently unrelated firms share a controller, cannot show a supervisor that the bank understood its exposure.

sections.heading: Network-led detection with explainable evidence
sections.body: The alternative is to build detection on resolved entities and their relationships. Entity resolution links customer, counterparty, device and corporate registry records that refer to the same real-world person or company, even when names, spellings and identifiers differ. On top of that resolved view, network analytics can surface clusters, shared attributes and flows that no single account reveals, and can prioritise alerts by the risk of the wider network rather than the size of one transaction. Platforms such as Quantexa are built around this approach, although the principle can be applied with several technologies. Explainability is the second requirement, and it is where many advanced models fall short. The same ACFE and SAS study found that 82 per cent of respondents prioritise explainability but only 6 per cent are confident explaining AI decisions. The CBUAE's February 2026 guidance on responsible AI reinforces the point, setting principles on transparency, explainability and human oversight. For the MLRO, every escalation or closure should be supported by a case record showing the entities involved, the relationships considered, the data sources used and the reasoning applied, in a form a supervisor can follow.

sections.heading: What MLROs and their boards should do now
sections.body: First, commission an independent assessment of what the current monitoring can and cannot see, testing it against network typologies such as mule rings, scam proceeds laundering and shared-control corporate structures, rather than only against the scenarios it was built for. Second, invest in entity resolution across customer, counterparty, payments and external registry data as a foundation, since both network detection and consistent screening depend on it. Third, layer network analytics over existing rules rather than replacing them in one step, and measure the change in the proportion of alerts that lead to meaningful outcomes. Fourth, re-examine exposures linked to Iraq and other newly listed jurisdictions through the resolved network view, not only through direct customer relationships. Fifth, integrate fraud and AML data and teams more closely, reflecting FATF's fraud focus and the reality that scam proceeds move over instant rails. Sixth, standardise the case record so that each decision is documented with its evidence and reasoning, and review a sample regularly at senior level. Finally, report to the board on detection effectiveness, not only alert volumes and backlogs. An MLRO who can demonstrate how the bank sees its risk is in a far stronger position than one who can only demonstrate that rules were run.

keyTakeaways: The CBUAE fined an MLRO AED 300,000 personally on 24 June 2026, alongside an AED 20 million fine on the bank.
FATF grey-listed Iraq in June 2026, and its new president has made fraud and scam-compound laundering his first priority.
Rules-based monitoring sees accounts in isolation; mule networks and shared-control structures require entity resolution and network analytics.
Explainable case records showing entities, relationships, data and reasoning are the MLRO's strongest evidence of effective control.

title: The Four-Hour Clock: Making Resilience Provable
subtitle: CBUAE's new operational risk regulation tests whether banks know, in hours, what has broken and why it matters
intro: The CBUAE Operational Risk Management Regulation, Circular C 1/2026, took effect on 14 September 2026 for all licensed financial institutions, replacing Circular 163/2018. Its most visible feature is a tiered incident-reporting clock, starting at four hours. A four-hour deadline cannot be met by convening a meeting to work out what is affected. It can only be met by an institution that already knows which operations are critical, what they depend on and how to see when they fail. The regulation, in short, turns operational resilience from a policy statement into a data capability.

sections.heading: What the regulation requires
sections.body: The regulation was communicated through a notice dated 24 July 2026, as reported by Crowe UAE, and applies to every licensed financial institution. As summarised in Gulf News coverage, it introduces tiered incident reporting: an initial notification within four hours where an incident has a significant impact on critical operations, a detailed report within 24 hours, and a 72-hour window for high-severity incidents. It also requires independent external penetration testing for critical functions. Institutions should work from the text in the CBUAE Rulebook for the precise triggers and content of each report, but the design intent is clear. The supervisor wants early, structured information about disruptions to the services that matter, followed quickly by a considered account of cause and impact. The penetration-testing requirement points the same way: the supervisor expects critical functions to be identified precisely enough to be tested independently. Both halves of the reporting requirement depend on information that most banks hold only in fragments across IT service management, security operations, vendor management and business continuity teams.

sections.heading: Why four hours changes the operating model
sections.body: In many institutions, incident reporting has been treated as a narrative exercise completed after the event. A four-hour clock reverses the sequence. Within that window someone must decide whether an incident affects a critical operation, whether the impact is significant, and what to tell the Central Bank, often while the technical teams are still diagnosing the fault. That decision is only as good as the information behind it. If the bank cannot quickly trace a failing server, application or supplier to the business services it supports, the incident manager is left guessing, and guesses tend to err in one of two directions: over-reporting, which erodes credibility with the supervisor, or under-reporting, which creates a far more serious problem later. The 24-hour detailed report compounds the pressure, because it requires a coherent account of scope, customer impact and root cause that is consistent with the initial notification. Institutions that treat these as communications tasks will struggle; those that treat them as data retrieval tasks will not.

sections.heading: Three data foundations behind provable resilience
sections.body: Meeting the clock reliably rests on three foundations. The first is a mapping of critical operations: each important business service linked to the processes, applications, infrastructure, data and people that deliver it, maintained as structured data rather than as diagrams in a continuity plan. The second is third-party dependency data. Critical operations increasingly run on cloud platforms, payment processors and software vendors, and the bank needs to know which suppliers, and which of their services, sit on each critical path, together with contractual notification terms that allow the bank to meet its own deadlines. The third is incident telemetry: monitoring signals from infrastructure, applications and security tools that can be correlated with the service map so that an alert on a component is immediately expressed as a potential impact on a named operation. When these three datasets share identifiers, the four-hour decision becomes a query. When they do not, it becomes a scramble. The same foundations also give the independent penetration testers a reliable scope for the critical functions they must test.

sections.heading: Sovereign infrastructure raises the bar further
sections.body: The regulation arrives as the UAE's financial infrastructure is being rebuilt. The Central Bank and Core42 launched a sovereign financial cloud on 25 February 2026 as part of the Financial Infrastructure Transformation programme, alongside the Digital Dirham, Open Finance and the Aani instant payments platform. Pinsent Masons observed in April 2026 that data residency, supervisory access and resilience duties are becoming increasingly operationalised in the wake of that launch. For banks, this means dependency mapping must cover where data and workloads physically reside and which shared national platforms sit on critical paths, not only which vendors are involved. It also means supervisory expectations of access to information are likely to rise rather than fall. An institution whose resilience evidence lives in slide decks and spreadsheets will find it hard to respond at the pace this environment implies. Making the underlying data governed and queryable is therefore both a compliance requirement and a practical defence against the next unannounced request.

sections.heading: What to do before the first reportable incident
sections.body: First, confirm the list of critical operations and have it approved at executive level, since every downstream decision depends on it. Second, build the service map as data: for each critical operation, record the applications, infrastructure, data stores, locations and suppliers it depends on, using identifiers shared with the configuration management database and the vendor register. Third, review contracts with suppliers on critical paths to ensure their notification obligations are short enough to let the bank meet a four-hour clock, and record those terms alongside the dependency. Fourth, connect monitoring and security telemetry to the service map so that alerts carry business context. A unified analytics platform such as Microsoft Fabric can host this correlation, though the platform matters less than the shared data model. Fifth, pre-build the four-hour notification and 24-hour report as templates populated from these sources, and rehearse them in tabletop exercises with the people who will actually be on call. Finally, report to the board on measures drawn from the data, such as mapping coverage of critical operations and the time taken in exercises to classify an incident. Resilience that can be shown in hours is resilience a supervisor can trust.

keyTakeaways: Circular C 1/2026 took effect on 14 September 2026, replacing Circular 163/2018 for all licensed financial institutions.
Tiered reporting starts at four hours for significant impact on critical operations, with 24-hour detailed and 72-hour high-severity windows.
Meeting the clock depends on three linked datasets: critical operations mapping, third-party dependencies and incident telemetry.
Pre-built, data-populated reports and rehearsed classification decisions turn the four-hour deadline from a scramble into a query.

title: After Reconciliation: The New CBUAE Law Demands Evidence
subtitle: FDL 6/2025's transition year is over. Supervisors will now ask banks to prove, not promise, compliance
intro: Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025, the new Central Bank law, came into force on 16 September 2025 with a one-year period for institutions to bring their affairs into line. That reconciliation period ended in mid-September 2026. The shift this creates is subtle but material: the question is no longer whether a bank has aligned its policies with the new law, but whether it can evidence, on request and at speed, that it operates within them. With responsible managers now personally liable, that evidence needs to be systematic rather than assembled by hand.

sections.heading: What changed on the reconciliation date
sections.body: The new law repealed the 2018 Central Bank law and the 2023 Insurance law, and Article 184 gave existing institutions one year to reconcile their status with it. According to Hadef & Partners, writing on 26 August 2026, the Central Bank's Board has the power to extend that period, but no general extension had been announced. Institutions should therefore assume they are now being supervised against the full framework. The perimeter has also moved. The law makes open finance, virtual-asset payments and digital wallets licensable activities, so business lines that grew up in a grey zone, including partnerships with third-party providers, now need to sit clearly inside a licence. Fines for carrying on unlicensed activity range from AED 50,000 to AED 500 million. For most banks the practical risk is not a deliberate breach but an activity, product or partnership that nobody mapped against the new licensing categories during the transition year.

sections.heading: Article 181 puts names next to controls
sections.body: The provision that should most concern executive committees is Article 181, under which responsible managers can be held personally liable. That changes the incentive structure inside a bank. A senior manager asked to attest that their area complies will reasonably want to see the evidence behind the attestation, not a summary slide. In many institutions that evidence is scattered: policies in a document repository, control test results in a governance, risk and compliance tool, operational data in core systems, and exceptions tracked in email. Personal liability turns this fragmentation from an efficiency problem into a governance one. The sensible response is to make the evidence chain from regulatory obligation to policy, control, test and result traceable in one place, so that any accountable manager can see the state of their controls without commissioning a project each time. That traceability is also what supervisors will look for when they test whether accountability is real or only documented.

sections.heading: The rulebook is still growing
sections.body: The law is a framework, and the Central Bank has continued to build on it through 2026. Hadef & Partners lists new regulations on insurance licensing in February, telemarketing in March and remuneration in April, alongside guidance on artificial intelligence and machine learning. That guidance note, published in February 2026, sets principles on governance and accountability, fairness, transparency and explainability, human oversight, and data management and privacy. It describes three oversight models, from human in the loop to human out of the loop, with the latter reserved for low-risk processes, requires disclosures in Arabic and English, gives customers rights to an explanation, to challenge and to redress, and confirms that institutions remain accountable for AI they outsource. Each new instrument adds obligations to the same inventory. Banks that manage compliance as a series of separate projects, one per circular, will find the overhead compounding; those that maintain a single, structured obligations register can absorb each new rule as an update rather than a programme.

sections.heading: Why compliance operations need automation now
sections.body: Moving from alignment to evidencing changes the workload profile of the compliance function. Alignment is front-loaded: gap analyses, policy rewrites and training. Evidencing is continuous: collecting control outputs, sampling transactions, reconciling data across systems, tracking remediation and producing packs for supervisors and boards. Done manually, this consumes the scarce specialist capacity that should be spent on judgement. Much of it is structured and repetitive, which makes it well suited to automation, whether through process automation platforms such as UiPath for collection and reconciliation tasks or through direct data pipelines from source systems. The prerequisite is a common control evidence layer: a governed data store in which obligations, controls, owners, test results and exceptions share identifiers and can be queried together. Without that layer, automation simply speeds up the production of disconnected artefacts. With it, the bank can answer supervisory requests from a single source, show accountable managers their current position and see where evidence is thin before someone else does.

sections.heading: Actions for the next two quarters
sections.body: First, complete a licensing perimeter check against the new law, product by product and partnership by partnership, with particular attention to open finance, wallets and any virtual-asset exposure, and record the outcome as a formal decision. Second, map each Article 181 accountable manager to the obligations and controls for which they could be held responsible, and give each of them a live view of control status and open exceptions. Third, build or consolidate the obligations register so that the 2026 regulations and the AI guidance sit alongside the law itself, each obligation linked to policies and controls. Fourth, stand up the control evidence layer, starting with the highest-risk domains, and connect it directly to source systems wherever possible so that evidence is generated rather than compiled. Fifth, target automation at the collection and reconciliation steps that currently absorb analyst time. Finally, agree with the board how assurance over the new framework will be reported, using measures that come straight from the evidence layer. The reconciliation year rewarded good intentions; the period that follows will reward institutions that can show their working.

keyTakeaways: FDL 6/2025's reconciliation period ended in mid-September 2026; no general extension had been announced as of late August.
Open finance, virtual-asset payments and digital wallets are licensable; unlicensed activity fines range from AED 50,000 to AED 500 million.
Article 181 personal liability means accountable managers need traceable evidence from obligation to control to test result.
A single control evidence layer is the prerequisite for automation; without it, automation just speeds up disconnected reporting.

title: After SAMA's mBridge Exit, Build for Many Rails
subtitle: GCC central banks are choosing different settlement paths. Banks should build to be indifferent to the choice
intro: On 20 September 2026 it was reported that the Saudi Central Bank had left mBridge, the multi-central-bank digital currency platform, after completing a proof of concept in May 2025. The UAE remains a participant. The temptation is to read this as a signal about which cross-border rail will win in the Gulf. That is the wrong lesson. The GCC's two largest economies are now on visibly different paths, and domestic and bilateral rails are multiplying. The right response for banks is not to bet on a rail but to build payments, treasury and compliance capabilities that work across all of them.

sections.heading: What happened, and what did not
sections.body: SAMA joined mBridge in June 2024 and, as reported, exited after completing a proof of concept on 13 May 2025, with the departure disclosed by the Financial Times on 20 September 2026. According to Fortune, the remaining participants are the central banks of China, Hong Kong, Thailand and the UAE, with Macau also reported as a member; the Bank for International Settlements itself stepped back from the project in October 2024. The Atlantic Council has estimated that transactions on the platform exceed US$55 billion. The UAE's commitment is concrete: on 11 November 2025 the Ministry of Finance and Dubai Finance completed the first government transaction in the Digital Dirham via mBridge, in under two minutes, and the 2025 Central Bank law makes the Digital Dirham legal tender. Commentary has framed the Saudi exit in geopolitical terms. For bank executives, the more useful observation is simpler: central bank choices about wholesale settlement infrastructure can change, may be disclosed long after the fact, and will not be synchronised across the region.

sections.heading: A region of multiplying rails
sections.body: mBridge is only one of several settlement paths now open to Gulf banks. The UAE's Aani instant payments platform reported 12.5 million users and 74 connected licensed financial institutions in April 2026, and its planned roadmap includes cross-border payments. The Al Etihad Payments company has selected Montran to build an international remittance gateway that links Aani first to India's UPI, with real-time ISO 20022 message transformation, a corridor serving roughly 3.5 million Indian nationals in the UAE. The Central Bank has approved a dirham-backed stablecoin, DDSC, which had processed more than Dh150 million by July 2026. In Saudi Arabia, electronic payments accounted for 85 per cent of retail payments in 2025, and SAMA moved open banking into formal licensing in March 2026. Add correspondent banking over Swift, and a mid-sized GCC bank may soon need to originate, receive, screen and reconcile value across five or six distinct rails, each with its own message formats, settlement timing, liquidity model and rulebook.

sections.heading: The risk is architectural lock-in
sections.body: Most bank payment architectures were designed around one dominant channel and extended piecemeal as new rails appeared. Each new connection typically brings its own gateway, its own data model, its own screening integration and its own reconciliation process. That approach was tolerable when new rails arrived once a decade. It is not tolerable when they arrive yearly and when a central bank can exit a platform after a pilot. The costs show up in three places. Operations teams reconcile the same customer activity across incompatible formats. Treasury loses a consolidated, intraday view of liquidity because positions sit in different systems with different cut-off logic. Compliance applies sanctions and transaction monitoring inconsistently, because each rail was integrated separately and at different times. The Saudi decision is a reminder that any single-rail investment carries switching risk. Institutions that have hard-wired their processes to one platform will pay twice: once to connect, and again to disconnect or re-route.

sections.heading: What a rail-agnostic bank looks like
sections.body: A rail-agnostic design separates what a payment is from how it travels. At its centre is a canonical payment data model based on ISO 20022, into which every inbound and outbound instruction is translated regardless of rail, much as the Aani to UPI gateway transforms messages in real time. Around that core sit thin adapters for each rail, so adding or retiring a connection is an integration task rather than a redesign. Treasury then works from one liquidity view across rails, with rules that route payments according to cost, speed, availability and counterparty reach. Compliance applies one set of screening and monitoring controls to the canonical record before and after routing, which means a sanctions decision or a suspicious-activity typology is consistent whether the value moves through Aani, a correspondent account, mBridge or a tokenised instrument. The structured data that ISO 20022 carries also improves screening quality and reconciliation, provided the bank preserves it end to end rather than truncating it at the edge of legacy systems.

sections.heading: Priorities for the next 12 months
sections.body: First, inventory every payment rail the bank uses or expects to use, and document for each its message standard, settlement model, liquidity requirements, screening integration and reconciliation process. The gaps between them are the business case. Second, adopt ISO 20022 as the internal canonical model, and stop adding rail-specific data structures to core systems. Third, consolidate sanctions screening and transaction monitoring so that they operate on the canonical record rather than per rail, and test that the same payment produces the same decision on every path. Fourth, give treasury an intraday, cross-rail liquidity view before volumes on newer rails become material. Fifth, prepare for cross-border instant corridors, starting with Aani to UPI, by modelling the remittance flows the bank already carries and the pricing, fraud and customer-experience implications of moving them to real-time rails. Finally, treat participation in any wholesale central bank platform as an option to be kept open through adapters, not a strategic commitment to be embedded in process. The region's settlement landscape will keep shifting; the banks that benefit will be those whose architecture does not need to shift with it.

keyTakeaways: SAMA's mBridge exit, reported on 20 September 2026, shows central bank settlement choices can diverge and change without warning.
GCC banks now face many rails: Aani, the Aani to UPI gateway, dirham stablecoins, mBridge, open banking and correspondent banking.
Adopt ISO 20022 as the canonical internal payment model, with thin adapters per rail, to avoid costly lock-in.
Apply one screening, monitoring and liquidity view across every rail so decisions are consistent wherever value travels.

author: ATS5E Research
title: Sovereign by Design
subtitle: Data platforms for the era of sovereign cloud, resilience supervision and quantum-safe banking
intro: Sovereign cloud, operational resilience supervision, personal-data enforcement and quantum readiness arrived in the GCC in the same year, and each asks the same questions: what does a bank hold, where does it sit, and what depends on it? CBUAE's Circular C 1/2026 sets a four-hour incident clock, SAMA wants a cryptographic inventory by 31 December 2026, and SDAIA has issued 48 PDPL enforcement decisions. Banks that answer each rule separately will build the same inventory five times. This whitepaper argues for one governed, residency-aware data platform, and sets out a regulation-to-data map, reference model, maturity scale and 12-month agenda.

sections.heading: Sovereignty became an engineering requirement
sections.body: In February 2026 CBUAE and Core42 launched a sovereign financial cloud as part of the Financial Infrastructure Transformation programme, alongside the Digital Dirham, Open Finance and Aani. Pinsent Masons has since described residency, supervisory access and resilience duties as becoming increasingly operationalised. For banks this marks a shift from attestation to evidence: a policy stating that data stays in the UAE is no longer enough without a live record of where each regulated dataset and every copy resides. The new Central Bank law, Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025, adds personal liability for responsible managers under Article 181, and its one-year reconciliation period ended in mid-September 2026. The common mistake is to treat residency as a hosting decision. Regulated data is copied into extracts, AI sandboxes, SaaS tools and test environments, and a bank's residency position is only as strong as its least-governed copy. Leaders should record residency as a data attribute and run a census of every copy.

sections.heading: One inventory, many regulators
sections.body: CBUAE's Operational Risk Management Regulation took effect on 14 September 2026, with an initial report due within four hours of an incident that significantly affects critical operations, a detailed report within 24 hours, a 72-hour window for high-severity incidents, and external penetration testing of critical functions. In Saudi Arabia, SDAIA issued 48 enforcement decisions over about a year, and SAMA's quantum circular requires a cryptographic inventory by 31 December 2026. Mapped side by side, these obligations call for five registers: a critical-operations map, a cryptographic inventory, a third-party register, a personal-data register and incident telemetry. All five are built from the same entities (asset, owner, location, dependency and classification). A bank that builds them separately pays for discovery five times and still cannot answer cross-cutting questions. A bank that builds one shared spine can answer those questions with a query.

sections.heading: Quantum-safe banking is a data problem first
sections.body: SAMA's circular on quantum computing risks, issued on 27 August 2026, requires KSA banks, finance companies, payment service companies and credit bureaus to inventory and classify cryptographic assets by 31 December 2026 and to complete an enterprise quantum-risk assessment by 31 March 2027, according to published summaries. The G7 Cyber Expert Group roadmap places discovery in 2027–28 and migration of critical systems in 2030–32, and SwiftNet 8.0 is expected to be post-quantum-enabled by 2027. Cryptography is spread across applications, certificates, libraries and vendor products, so an inventory is only useful if it links each asset to the system it protects, the classification of the data involved and the provider that controls it. Built as a governed data product rather than a one-off spreadsheet, the inventory becomes the migration plan and can be reused for board reporting, SwiftNet planning and penetration test scoping.

sections.heading: In-region compute and the reference model
sections.body: In-region AI capacity is narrowing the old trade-off between leading models and data residency. Microsoft has committed US$15.2bn to the UAE between 2023 and 2029, G42 has set out plans for Stargate UAE, and HUMAIN is targeting 1.9GW in Saudi Arabia by 2030, from a national base of 467MW in early 2026. As compute stops being the constraint, supervisors will focus on the data: what fed a model, where it was processed and whether consent covered that purpose. The paper sets out a six-layer reference model: a sovereign landing zone, a governed lakehouse, active metadata and lineage, regulatory data products, controls as code, and consumption. It also sets out a five-level maturity scale tested against the four-hour report. Gartner finds that culture, not funding, is the main reason governance fails, so ownership of data products must sit in the business.

keyTakeaways: Sovereignty, operational resilience and data governance are now one engineering problem: every GCC rule asks what a bank holds, where it sits and what depends on it.
CBUAE's four-hour incident clock and SAMA's 31 December 2026 cryptographic inventory deadline cannot be met with manually maintained spreadsheets.
Build one shared inventory spine and serve each regulatory register as a view of it, instead of running five separate compliance projects.
In-region AI compute shifts the residency challenge from infrastructure to lineage; culture and business ownership decide whether governance holds.

title: Open Money
subtitle: Open finance, instant rails and tokenised dirhams: rebuilding the GCC payments stack
intro: Between November 2025 and September 2026 the GCC payments stack changed at every layer. UAE Open Finance went live, SAMA moved open banking to formal licensing, Aani reached 12.5 million users, dirham-backed stablecoins began settling real transactions, the first government Digital Dirham payment cleared in under two minutes, and Saudi Arabia and the UAE took different paths on mBridge. Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025 made open finance, virtual-asset payments and wallets licensable. This whitepaper argues that banks now face a choice: become dumb pipes on every rail, or build the orchestration and trust layer that makes every payment safe, reconciled and funded.

sections.heading: Every layer moved at once
sections.body: Access, rails, instruments, infrastructure and law all changed within the same year. FAB and Pay10, Commercial Bank of Dubai and ADIB took UAE Open Finance into live operation, with Nebras overseeing connectivity and governance. SAMA moved open banking from sandbox to formal licensing on 26 March 2026. Aani scaled and is being linked to India's UPI. DDSC, AE Coin and RAKBANK's planned token brought dirham stablecoins into the market, while the CBUAE and Core42 launched a sovereign financial cloud as part of the Financial Infrastructure Transformation programme alongside the Digital Dirham, Open Finance and Aani. The paper maps each rail and instrument, its confirmed status and what it means for banks. The most common mistake is treating these as five separate programmes with five budgets. None of them then owns the question that matters: where the bank will sit in the flow of money once all of them are live.

sections.heading: Open access and instant rails
sections.body: UAE Open Finance is now production traffic, and FDL 6/2025 legitimises new licensed competitors between customer and account while giving banks their own licensed route to compete. In Saudi Arabia, the Open Banking Forum on 16 September 2026 set bank readiness for Payment Initiation Services as the next priority, in a market where 85% of retail payments were electronic in 2025. Aani now has 12.5 million users, an average transfer time of three seconds, around 774,000 merchants and 74 connected institutions, and a Montran-built gateway will link it to UPI with real-time ISO 20022 transformation. Instant, irrevocable payments remove the settlement window banks once used to catch fraud, balance liquidity and repair data, so every control must now run in real time.

sections.heading: Programmable money and diverging settlement
sections.body: DDSC has completed a Dh110m transaction and processed more than Dh150m since launch; AE Coin is licensed and RAKBANK has in-principle approval for an AED stablecoin. The Digital Dirham is legal tender under the new Central Bank Law, and the first government transaction settled via mBridge in under two minutes. Cross-border settlement is diverging: SAMA exited mBridge after a proof of concept, as reported, while the UAE remains a participant. A bank that neither issues nor custodies tokens sees only the fiat edges of a transaction, which is the dumb-pipe risk in its purest form. Banks should plan for wholesale and government use first, and make sure they can reconcile tokenised money when it reaches the balance sheet. For banks active in both the UAE and KSA, treasury and settlement must be designed for several cross-border models at once.

sections.heading: Choosing a role and building the orchestration layer
sections.body: UAE APP scam losses are projected to rise from US$8.3m in 2023 to US$30.3m by 2028, and one in five victims leave their bank, so fraud is where the pipe leaks first. With FDL 6/2025's reconciliation period over and managers personally liable, every role carries a licence footprint. The paper sets out four roles: rail participant, experience owner, orchestrator and infrastructure provider. It warns against becoming a rail participant by default. Winning banks build five capabilities: a rail-agnostic payment hub, ISO 20022-native data, real-time fraud controls deployed with every rail, reconciliation across fiat and tokenised settlement, and liquidity management across rails. Each can be built incrementally on today's estate. A 90-day, 6-month and 12-month agenda maps these moves to the 5E framework.

keyTakeaways: The GCC payments stack changed at every layer in under twelve months, from open-finance access to tokenised settlement, so it needs one owner and one map.
Instant rails such as Aani, now at 12.5 million users, remove the settlement window, so fraud, screening and liquidity controls must run in real time.
Dirham stablecoins and the Digital Dirham make reconciliation across fiat and tokenised ledgers a core capability rather than an experiment.
Banks that do not choose a role deliberately become rail participants by default, carrying fraud and liquidity risk without owning the value.
