title: SAMA's Quantum Circular Is a Data Problem
subtitle: The 31 December cryptographic inventory will be won by data engineering, not by cryptographers
intro: On 27 August 2026 SAMA issued its circular on enhancing operational resilience against quantum computing risks. According to published summaries, Saudi banks, finance companies, payment service companies and credit bureaus must complete a cryptographic asset inventory and classification by 31 December 2026. Most institutions will hand this to their cryptography specialists. That is a mistake. The hard part is not knowing which algorithms are vulnerable; it is finding every place they are used, who owns them and what data they protect. That is a data problem, and it should be run as one.

sections.heading: What SAMA has asked for, and how early it is
sections.body: According to published summaries of the circular, the obligations are sequenced. The cryptographic asset inventory and its classification are due by 31 December 2026. An enterprise-wide quantum-risk assessment follows by 31 March 2027. Quantum risk becomes a standing item on the Board Risk Committee agenda, institutions may document compensating controls or planned decommissioning where migration is not immediately feasible, and third-party dependencies must be identified. The timing matters. The G7 Cyber Expert Group roadmap published in January 2026 places discovery and inventory in 2027 to 2028, migration of critical systems in 2030 to 2032 and full validation in 2034 to 2035. SAMA has therefore pulled the discovery phase forward by roughly a year relative to that international reference point. Saudi institutions will be among the first anywhere to be supervised against a completed inventory, which means there is little peer practice to copy and every reason to design the work properly from the start rather than treat it as a one-off questionnaire.

sections.heading: Why this is a data problem, not a cryptography problem
sections.body: The list of algorithms considered vulnerable to a future quantum computer is short and well understood. The list of places those algorithms live inside a bank is long and poorly documented. Cryptography sits in TLS certificates on internet-facing and internal services, in hardware security modules, in card and payment switches, in code-signing, in VPNs and in database encryption. It is also embedded in libraries inside application code and in vendor products whose configuration the bank does not directly control. None of this is recorded in one place. Certificate management tools see some of it, the CMDB sees some of it, network scanning sees some of it, and procurement records hold the only trace of what sits inside third-party software. Producing a defensible inventory means ingesting these sources, resolving the same asset appearing under different names, linking each cryptographic instance to an application, a business owner and the data it protects, and keeping that picture current as systems change. That is entity resolution, lineage and data quality work. Institutions that staff it only with security engineers will produce a spreadsheet; institutions that staff it with data engineers alongside will produce an asset.

sections.heading: Classification is where the risk judgement actually lives
sections.body: An inventory without classification tells the Board Risk Committee very little. The useful question is not which systems use a vulnerable algorithm, since most will, but which ones protect data that must remain confidential for many years. Encrypted material captured today can be stored and decrypted later if the underlying scheme is broken, so long-lived data such as customer identity records, credit histories, account data and interbank messaging deserves priority over short-lived session traffic. Classification therefore needs attributes that security tooling does not usually hold: data sensitivity, retention period, regulatory obligations, business criticality and whether the system supports a critical operation. Much of that already exists in data governance catalogues and privacy records, not least because personal-data protection obligations already require banks to know what they hold and why. Joining the cryptographic inventory to the existing data catalogue is the fastest route to a classification that the March 2027 risk assessment can actually rely on.

sections.heading: Third parties and messaging will set the real pace
sections.body: The requirement to identify third-party dependencies is the part most likely to be underestimated. A large share of a bank's cryptography is supplied by vendors: core banking platforms, payment processors, cloud services, HSM providers and messaging networks. The bank cannot migrate what its suppliers have not yet upgraded, but it can document the dependency, obtain each supplier's roadmap and record a compensating control or decommissioning plan where the circular permits one. Interbank messaging is a useful example of an externally set clock. SwiftNet 8.0 is expected to be post-quantum-enabled by 2027, with a 15-month migration window. Institutions that know exactly which internal systems generate, sign and consume those messages will be able to plan that migration calmly; those that do not will find the window short. The same logic applies to every critical supplier, and it argues for turning the third-party register into a live, queryable dataset rather than a set of contract files.

sections.heading: What CISOs and CROs should do in the next 90 days
sections.body: The period between now and 31 December allows for one disciplined pass, not several. First, agree a single data model for a cryptographic asset before discovery starts: location, algorithm, key length, certificate or key lifetime, owning application, business owner, supplier, data protected and critical-operation flag. Second, run automated discovery across certificate stores, network traffic, code repositories, HSMs and cloud key management, and load the results into one governed store rather than separate team spreadsheets. Third, resolve and enrich: deduplicate assets, link them to the application inventory and the data catalogue, and attach sensitivity and retention attributes. Fourth, send a structured request to every critical supplier for its cryptographic components and post-quantum roadmap, and record the answers against the same model. Fifth, agree with the Board Risk Committee how quantum risk will be reported each quarter, using measures drawn directly from the inventory, such as the share of critical operations mapped and the share of long-lived data on vulnerable schemes. Finally, assign an accountable owner who spans the CISO and chief data officer functions. The inventory will be judged on its completeness and currency, and both depend on data ownership more than cryptographic expertise.

keyTakeaways: SAMA's circular requires a cryptographic inventory and classification by 31 December 2026, roughly a year ahead of the G7 discovery timeline.
Finding and linking cryptographic assets across systems and suppliers is entity-resolution and lineage work; staff it with data engineers.
Classify by data shelf-life and critical-operation support, reusing the existing data catalogue, to prepare for the March 2027 risk assessment.
Treat third-party cryptography and SwiftNet 8.0 migration as externally set clocks and capture supplier roadmaps now.

author: ATS5E Research
title: Agents Under Supervision
subtitle: Deploying agentic AI in GCC banks under the new wave of AI rules
intro: In 2026, AI governance in GCC finance moved from voluntary principle to supervisory expectation. The CBUAE set out three oversight models for AI, SDAIA published a national AI risk framework, the EU fixed new high-risk deadlines and the FSB consulted on sound practices. At the same moment, AI agents began initiating payments in the UAE and banks started competing publicly on AI. This paper argues that treating governance as an approval gate will stall agentic AI, and sets out a supervisable agent architecture, a four-level maturity model and a 90-day to 12-month agenda for GCC bank leaders.

sections.heading: The year AI governance became supervisory
sections.body: The CBUAE's February 2026 guidance note on responsible AI is principles-based but specific. It describes three oversight models, human in the loop, human on the loop and human out of the loop, with the last reserved for low-risk processes. It gives customers rights to explanation, challenge and redress, expects disclosures in Arabic and English, and keeps banks accountable for outsourced AI. The DFSA's 2025 survey found 52% of DIFC firms using AI but 21% lacking clear accountability for it. In Saudi Arabia, SDAIA's framework introduces a four-by-four likelihood-impact matrix and seven risk categories. For banks with EU exposure, the Digital Omnibus moves stand-alone high-risk systems, including credit scoring, to a 2 December 2027 deadline, while the FSB's twelve sound practices are expected in final form in October 2026. Supervisors can now ask banks to prove how their AI is controlled.

sections.heading: Agents are already transacting
sections.body: Agentic AI in the Gulf has reached live payments. Visa reported working with Aldar so UAE customers can use AI agents to pay recurring real-estate service charges, and Mastercard launched Agent Pay in the UAE with Majid Al Futtaim. Banks are also competing openly on AI: the inaugural Evident AI Index for Banks in the Middle East and Africa ranked Emirates NBD first of 25, with transparency scored as a pillar. ADIB appointed a Chief AI Officer to deploy generative and agentic AI. Evident found the regional AI talent pool is about half the size of global bank benchmarks, which means oversight cannot rely on adding reviewers. BCG estimates AI agents could lift retail-bank profitability by 30% by 2030, but that prize will go to banks that can show how their agents are supervised.

sections.heading: Why governance as a gate will fail
sections.body: The instinctive response to new rules is an approval committee. That model breaks for agents: they change behaviour after approval, approvals do not produce evidence of why a specific action was taken, and review queues become the bottleneck. Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027, and separately finds that culture, not funding, is the main reason governance fails. The ACFE and SAS found that 82% of anti-fraud professionals prioritise explainability, yet only 6% are confident explaining AI decisions. Explanation has to be engineered into how systems record decisions, and product teams need to own their controls rather than hand governance to someone else after the build. Banks should stop any pilot that has no clear route to production-grade logging and oversight.

sections.heading: The supervisable agent architecture and maturity model
sections.body: ATS5E proposes five components: a live agent inventory with risk tiers mapped to the CBUAE oversight models and SDAIA's matrix; structured decision logging that makes explanation and redress practicable; human-on-the-loop operations with thresholds and pause controls; accountability for vendor and partner agents; and versioned bilingual disclosure. The paper maps CBUAE, SDAIA, EU AI Act and FSB obligations to concrete controls, and offers a four-level maturity model from Experimental to Supervisable at scale. It also addresses residency: decision logs are regulated data, and with the CBUAE sovereign financial cloud and expanding UAE and Saudi compute, agent platforms should be portable across in-country options. A 90-day, six-month and twelve-month agenda ties each step to the 5E framework, starting with named owners and a complete inventory.

keyTakeaways: The CBUAE's three oversight models give banks a ready structure for tiering agents; human out of the loop is for low-risk processes only.
Accountability is the first supervisory question: 21% of DIFC firms lack clear AI accountability, and banks remain responsible for outsourced AI.
Governance as an approval gate will not scale to agents; controls must be built into the agent and owned by product teams.
Decision logging, human-on-the-loop operations and bilingual disclosure turn regulatory principles into evidence a supervisor can inspect.
